title: Crowns and presence (Berakhot 17a)
hookLine: in the world to come there's no eating or drinking; the righteous sit with crowns and enjoy the Presence
tomorrow: a teacher makes a student stand all lesson long. then what?

cards: At some concerts, they lock your phone in a pouch at the door. For the first few minutes, people don't know what to do with their hands. Then something shifts, and they're just there.
Rav had a favorite saying about the world to come, and it strips away far more than a phone. No food, no rivals, no deadlines. So what is left?
Something you can't eat and can't win.

teach.b: Here's Rav's saying, in plain words. The world to come is not like this world.
There's no eating and no drinking there, no having children, no business, no jealousy, no hatred, no competition.

teach.h: CROWNS, AND THE RADIANCE OF THE PRESENCE.
teach.b: Instead, the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah, God's presence. Then he gives a verse.
When the elders went up the mountain with Moses, Exodus says "they beheld God, and did eat and drink."
Rav reads it this way: the beholding was their food and drink.
The presence itself fed them. Now look again at what's gone from his list. Not only hunger.
Jealousy, hatred, competition: the whole engine of comparing. Nobody's checking whose crown is shinier. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight.
In this picture, the reward isn't a feast or a prize ceremony. It's being fully present, with nothing to earn. Rav's is one picture of the world to come among several in Jewish teaching.
But it turns a quiet question back on this world: if presence is what lasts, how much of it is getting crowded out?

how: Jewish teaching speaks of olam haba, the world to come, in several ways; Rav's saying about the righteous enjoying the radiance of the Shechinah is one picture of it that is often studied.

o: a festival meal held in the Temple at harvest time
gold crowns handed out to the winning scholars
the world to come as pure presence with God, no rivals

games.q: Rav's world to come — tap the pairs.

s: Judaism has no teaching about a world to come
the Talmud speaks of the world to come; Rav's saying is one picture of it.
Rav pictures the world to come as an endless banquet
no eating or drinking: beholding God's presence is the food.
Rav's list of what's gone includes jealousy and competition
no jealousy, no hatred, no competition.

games.q: your little brother asks if the world to come has pizza and video games. using Rav's picture, what could you say?
o: Rav pictured no food or games, but being with God, with no fighting at all.
Rav said it's whatever you liked best here, forever, as much as you want.
Rav said no one can say anything about it, so it's better not to ask.
games.why: Rav: no eating or drinking, no jealousy or competition; the righteous sit with crowns and enjoy the radiance of the Presence.

practice: Put down whatever is in your hands. For the rest of the sit, only take in this room: one sound, the light on one surface, the weight of your body where you sit. No task and no score, just being here.

wordCard.voice: Crowns and presence. Rav's world to come: no food, no rivals, the righteous crowned and fed by the radiance of the Shechinah.

orig.note: Hebrew: the radiance of the Shechinah, God's presence, which the righteous enjoy in Rav's saying.

carryVoice: Crowns and presence: that's the line, with nothing to earn and nobody to beat. Fifteen of fifty in Berakhot.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (Rav's favorite saying: the world to come is not like this world…)

sources.q: they beheld God, and did eat and drink
